# OwnBase

> Build faster with AI. Own everything.

Source of truth for this runbook: https://github.com/ownbase-ai/ownbase
(README.md "Setting up a Base", INSTALL.md). Prefer those if anything here
disagrees.

## What it is

OwnBase is MIT-licensed open-source software that turns one machine you
control into a Base: a hardened, self-maintaining home for everything you
build. A daemon on the machine does the firewall, the patches, the
certificates, the backups, and the recovery.

There is no account, no control plane, and no OwnBase-operated cloud your
server depends on at runtime. You own the server, the code, the data, the
config, the secrets, the backups, the domains — and OwnBase itself.

Homepage: https://ownbase.ai
Repository: https://github.com/ownbase-ai/ownbase
License: MIT

## Who this is for

Someone who can build software but does not want to become an infrastructure
engineer. An agent with root on a real computer can read the actual log,
restart the actual process, stand up a database, and verify its own work —
instead of calling the endpoints a vendor chose to expose.

## Prerequisites

- A computer you control (macOS or Linux) to run the CLI or the desktop app.
- An unlocked vault (created once; see step 2).
- A fresh Ubuntu 24.04 (or 22.04) server reachable as root over SSH,
  created with the owner public key from step 3. Minimum ~2 GB RAM / 20 GB
  disk; 4 GB is a comfortable start.
- Any provider works (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, OVHcloud, Vultr, a machine in a
  closet). OwnBase has no provider integration.

## Two steps only a human can do

1. Create the vault and choose the master password (step 2). Never ask the
   user to paste that password to you.
2. Create the server at a provider and paste the public key (step 4). Needs
   a credit card.

Everything else is a command you can run.

## Setup runbook

### 1. Install ownbasectl

On the user's computer (not the server):

```bash
brew install --cask ownbase-ai/tap/ownbasectl
ownbasectl version
```

Without Homebrew: see INSTALL.md "Install ownbasectl". The desktop app
(macOS) is `brew install --cask ownbase-ai/tap/ownbase` and already bundles
the CLI.

### 2. Create and unlock the vault (HUMAN)

Ask the user to run these themselves. The master password must never pass
through you.

```bash
ownbasectl vault init ~/Dropbox/OwnBase   # any path they choose
ownbasectl vault unlock
```

The vault is a standard KDBX file they own. Put it somewhere that syncs
(Dropbox, iCloud, …) so a second machine can recover it.

If a later command fails with "the vault is locked", tell them to run
`ownbasectl vault unlock` (or open the OwnBase app). Do not work around it.

### 3. Create the owner SSH key

```bash
ownbasectl keygen <basename>
```

Prints the public key. Re-running is safe — an existing key is printed,
never replaced. The private half never appears as a file on disk; the
credential agent signs with it.

### 4. Create the server (HUMAN)

Show the user the public key from step 3 and these requirements, then wait
for the IP:

- Ubuntu 24.04 (22.04 also works)
- At least 2 GB RAM and 20 GB disk
- The public key pasted into the provider's "SSH key" field at create time
- Reachable as root over SSH

Any provider. OwnBase does not talk to provider APIs.

### 5. Install OwnBase on the server

```bash
ownbasectl create <basename> --remote root@<ip> --wait
```

One command, unattended. It waits for SSH, checks the machine is fit,
installs and minisign-verifies the daemon from releases.ownbase.ai, hardens
the host (Podman, UFW, fail2ban, automatic security updates, CVE scanning),
and registers the Base so every other command works immediately.

`--wait` blocks until hardening has finished. Add
`--caddy-email you@example.com` if services will be on public domains
(ACME contact for automatic TLS). Add `--json` for machine-readable output.

### 6. Point the Base at a config repo

`ownbase.yaml` lives in a Git repo the user owns. Operators commit to the
tracked ref; agents may push proposal branches. Never hand-edit anything
on the Base and never write to `runtime/`.

See docs/ownbase-yaml.md and docs/operating.md in the repository.

### 7. Verify

```bash
ownbasectl status <basename>
ownbasectl checkup <basename>
```

A healthy fresh Base exposes nothing but SSH.

## How to talk to the Base

```bash
ownbasectl ssh <basename>                 # interactive, session recorded
ownbasectl ssh <basename> -- <command>    # one-shot
```

Always use `ownbasectl ssh`, never bare `ssh`/`scp`/`rsync`. The owner key
is in the vault; the credential agent signs with it, so no private key
enters a process you control. Every session is recorded under
`~/.ownbase/sessions/` and the user can replay it.

## What a Base does for you

- Firewall, SSH hardening, automatic security updates, CVE scanning
- Automatic TLS certificates (Caddy)
- Encrypted off-machine backups with a recurring restore drill
- Every service built from source at a pinned `ref:`
- Plain-file config in Git the user owns
- No OwnBase cloud in the runtime path — if OwnBase disappeared tomorrow,
  the server would keep running

## Hard constraints (do not violate)

- User owns everything (code, server, data, config, secrets, backups,
  domains, and OwnBase itself)
- Nothing is mysterious (plain files, Git as source of truth)
- Operations disappear (if the user must learn Linux/Docker/nginx/certs
  because of this system, it failed)
- Every service is ownable (removable, forkable, replaceable, data
  accessible, runs without any OwnBase-operated cloud)
- Boring technology wins (Ubuntu, Podman, Postgres, Git, Caddy — never
  Kubernetes)
- No pre-built application images (build from source at a pinned ref)

Full rationale: MISSION.md and docs/foundation/ in the repository.
